open: Nearly two thousand years ago, about a hundred thousand people lived in this city. <break time="0.8s" /> Its builders laid it out on one grid, turned fifteen and a half degrees east of north. <break time="0.8s" /> They planned in straight lines and right angles. So how did they measure?
lidar: In 2015, airborne lidar mapped a hundred and sixty-five square kilometers of the valley. <break time="0.8s" /> About 60 percent of that ground has been reshaped in modern times. <break time="0.8s" /> Many of the new fields and roads still follow the ancient grid. <break time="0.8s" /> This is not a lost city waiting to be found. It is a known city under a living one.
question: So ask a different question: not where, but how it was designed. <break time="0.8s" /> Did its builders share a standard unit of length? <break time="0.8s" /> Proposals include 83 centimeters, about eighty and a half centimeters and about 58 centimeters. Or none at all. <break time="0.8s" /> After three decades, there is still no consensus.
read: The evidence may already exist, in three-D AutoCAD plans from the excavations. <break time="0.8s" /> Step one. Convert each drawing, keep every layer, and rotate it onto the fifteen-and-a-half-degree grid.
extract: Step two. Software pulls out every dimension a builder would have set out. <break time="0.8s" /> Wall thicknesses. Room widths. Stair treads. Talud and tablero heights. <break time="0.8s" /> Each number links back to the line it came from.
curate: Step three. The archaeologist tags each one as original, restored or eroded, and by phase. <break time="0.8s" /> Blind. Nobody sees which unit fits while tagging. <break time="0.8s" /> Step four. Freeze the data, code and hypotheses, and pre-register them.
test: Step five. Wrap every length around a circle one candidate unit long. <break time="0.8s" /> If they share that unit, they bunch up at one point. <break time="0.8s" /> Sweep from 30 centimeters to two meters. A real unit rises above the noise. <break time="0.8s" /> Its half-unit echoes too, and the analysis has to decide between them.
attack: Step six. AI skeptic agents try to explain each result away. <break time="0.8s" /> Drafting rounding. Modern restoration. Stairs sized to feet. Lucky calendar numbers. <break time="0.8s" /> Each objection becomes a check that runs before anyone believes the peak.
store: Step seven. Store the lidar like evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> The raw point clouds stay on an encrypted lab drive, never on a public cloud. <break time="0.8s" /> Every tile is saved in an open format and fingerprinted, so each result can name the exact data it used. <break time="0.8s" /> Only derived numbers ever leave the vault.
process: Step eight. Turn millions of points into a bare-earth surface. <break time="0.8s" /> Ground filtering strips away houses and trees. Relief models make low walls and terraces stand out. <break time="0.8s" /> A line detector then finds every edge that runs with the city’s grid. <break time="0.8s" /> And a classifier trained on the team’s own ground-checked map sorts ancient lines from modern ones.
city: Step nine. Measure the city. <break time="0.8s" /> Take the ancient lines and measure the gaps between parallel walls, from ten to five hundred meters. <break time="0.8s" /> Then run the same test, and ask whether streets and buildings share one unit.
ai: So what does the AI actually bring? <break time="0.8s" /> It builds: the CAD reader, the lidar pipeline and the statistics, each with tests. <break time="0.8s" /> It reads: Spanish layer names, field notes and old reports become tidy tables. <break time="0.8s" /> It remembers: every published dimension of the city, gathered into a second dataset. <break time="0.8s" /> And it doubts: skeptic agents attack each result before a reviewer can.
guard: Just as important is where the AI stops. <break time="0.8s" /> It never decides what is ancient. The archaeologist confirms every tag it proposes. <break time="0.8s" /> It never sees coordinates or imagery, only lengths and labels. <break time="0.8s" /> Every prompt and script is logged, and the final statistics run without any AI at all.
team: The archaeologist knows which stones are original, and what an answer would mean. <break time="0.8s" /> The lidar engineer owns the vault and the pipeline. <break time="0.8s" /> And Claude does the heavy lifting in between.
outcomes: 83 centimeters holds. A different unit fits. The unit drifts over time. Or there was none. <break time="0.8s" /> Because the test is fixed in advance, every result is publishable.
next: Weeks one and two: prove the method on synthetic buildings. <break time="0.8s" /> Weeks three to six: one structure, end to end. <break time="0.8s" /> Then the full corpus, the test, and the city.
